Prominent political events
Africa
• <color=#3366CC>African National Congress</color> leader <color=#3366CC>Nelson Mandela</color> was released from prison on 11 February 1990, after thirty years
of imprisonment for opposing apartheid and white-minority rule in South Africa. Apartheid ended in South Africa in
• Nelson Mandela was elected President of South Africa in 1994, becoming the first democratically elected president
in South African history, and ending a long legacy of apartheid white rule in the country.
Americas
• The Argentine peso was pegged to the <color=#3366CC>American dollar</color> by the Convertibility plan by the government of <color=#3366CC>Carlos</color>
<color=#3366CC>Menem</color> in an attempt to eliminate <color=#3366CC>hyperinflation</color> and stimulate <color=#3366CC>economic growth</color>. While it was initially met with
considerable success, the board's actions ultimately failed. The Convertibility Plan went from 1991 to 2002.
• The establishment of the <color=#3366CC>North American Free Trade Agreement</color> (NAFTA) on 1 January 1994, created a North
American free-trade zone consisting of Canada, Mexico, and the United States.
• The Constitution of Argentina went through an important reform in 1994, which introduced <color=#3366CC>third generation rights</color>,
gave more relevance to <color=#3366CC>international treaties</color>, and also introduced new concepts such as Necessity and Urgency
Decrees and the two-round system.
• Canadian politics was radically altered in the 1993 federal election with the collapse of the Progressive
Conservative Party of Canada. A major political party in Canada since 1867, the party went from controlling the
government to being left with only two seats. The New Democratic Party collapsed as well, with their sets declining
from 44 to 9. The Liberal Party of Canada was the only genuinely 'national' political party left standing. Regionally
based parties, such as the Quebec-based Bloc Québécois and the almost entirely Western Canada-based Reform
Party of Canada, rose from political insignificance to being major political parties.
• After the collapse of the Meech Lake constitutional accord in 1990, the province of <color=#3366CC>Quebec</color> in Canada experienced
a rekindled wave of separatism by <color=#3366CC>Francophone</color> Québécois nationalists, who sought for Quebec to become an
independent country and forced a referendum on the question of independence in 1995.
• The 1995 Quebec referendum on sovereignty was held in the predominantly francophone province of Quebec in
Canada, a majority Anglophone country. If accepted, Quebec would have become an independent country with an
economic association with Canada. Quebec's voters narrowly rejected the proposal.
• <color=#3366CC>Jean-Bertrand Aristide</color>, a former Haitian priest, became the first democratically elected President of <color=#3366CC>Haiti</color> in 1990. A
proponent of liberation theology, Aristide was appointed to a Roman Catholic parish in <color=#3366CC>Port-au-Prince</color> in 1982 after
completing his studies to become a priest of the Salesian order. Aristide was later forced into exile in the Central
African Republic and South Africa and returned to Haiti after several years.
• <color=#3366CC>Ernesto Zedillo</color> was elected President of Mexico in the 1994 presidential election, making him the last of an
uninterrupted 72-year-long succession of Mexican presidents from the dominant <color=#3366CC>Institutional Revolutionary Party</color>
(PRI). The original PRI candidate, Luis Donaldo Colosio Murrieta, was assassinated several months prior.
• Due to <color=#3366CC>internal conflict</color> and an economic crisis, <color=#3366CC>Alberto Fujimori</color> rose to power in <color=#3366CC>Peru</color> and remained in office for
eleven years. His administration was marked by economic development but also by numerous human rights
violations (La Cantuta massacre, Barrios Altos massacre) and a rampant corruption network set up by Vladimiro
Montesinos.

• The sluggish <color=#3366CC>Latin American</color> economies of <color=#3366CC>Argentina</color>, <color=#3366CC>Brazil</color>, <color=#3366CC>Chile</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Mexico</color>, by a new emphasis on <color=#3366CC>free</color>
<color=#3366CC>markets</color> for all their citizens after the debt crisis of the 1980s. Following democratic reforms and neoliberal policies
were implemented by President <color=#3366CC>Carlos Saúl Menem</color> (Argentina), President <color=#3366CC>Eduardo Frei Ruiz-Tagle</color> (Chile),
President <color=#3366CC>Ernesto Zedillo</color> (Mexico), and President <color=#3366CC>Fernando Henrique Cardoso</color> (Brazil), in their best shape by the
late 1990s.
• <color=#3366CC>United States President</color> Bill Clinton was a dominant political figure in international affairs during the 1990s, known
primarily for his attempts to negotiate peace in the Middle East and end the ongoing wars occurring in the former
Yugoslavia, his promotion of international action to decrease human-created <color=#3366CC>climate change</color>, and his endorsement
of advancing <color=#3366CC>free trade</color> in the Americas.
• After a failed coup attempt in 1992, <color=#3366CC>Hugo Chávez</color>, politician and former member of the Venezuelan military, is
elected President of <color=#3366CC>Venezuela</color> in 1998.
• Lewinsky scandal – US president Bill Clinton was caught in a media-frenzied scandal involving inappropriate
relations with White House intern Monica Lewinsky, which was first announced on 21 January 1998. After the
United States House of Representatives impeached Bill Clinton on 19 December 1998, for perjury under oath, and
following an investigation by federal prosecutor <color=#3366CC>Kenneth Starr</color>, the Senate acquitted Clinton of all charges on 12
February 1999. He served out the remainder of his second term.
• California voters passed Proposition 215 in 1996, which legalized <color=#3366CC>cannabis</color> for medicinal purposes.
Asia
• In 1990, the <color=#3366CC>Lebanese Civil War</color> came to a close and a return to political normalcy in <color=#3366CC>Lebanon</color> began. With peace
among all factions in Lebanon, the rebuilding of the country and its capital, <color=#3366CC>Beirut</color>, began.
• 1990 Nepalese revolution, a multiparty movement against the one-party Panchayat rule in Nepal. It led to the end
of absolute monarchy in Nepal and the restoration of democracy.
• <color=#3366CC>Israeli</color> Prime Minister <color=#3366CC>Yitzhak Rabin</color> and Palestinian Prime Minister <color=#3366CC>Yasser Arafat</color> agree to the Israeli–Palestinian
peace process at the culmination of the Oslo Accords, negotiated by the United States president, Bill Clinton, on 13
September 1993.
• By signing the Oslo accords, the <color=#3366CC>Palestine Liberation Organization</color> recognized Israel's right to exist. At the same
time, Israel permitted the creation of an autonomous Palestinian National Authority consisting of the <color=#3366CC>Gaza Strip</color> and
<color=#3366CC>West Bank</color>, which was implemented in 1994.
• Israeli military forces withdrew from these Palestinian territories in compliance with the accord, which marked the
end of the <color=#3366CC>First Intifada</color> (a period of violence between Palestinian Arab militants and Israeli armed forces from 1987
• The Palestinian National Authority was created in 1994 following the Oslo Accords, giving Palestinian Arab people
official autonomy over the Gaza Strip and West Bank, though not official independence from Israel.
• On 4 November 1995, Israeli prime minister Yitzhak Rabin <color=#3366CC>was assassinated</color> by a right-wing extremist who
opposed the signing of the Oslo Accords.
• North Yemen and South Yemen <color=#3366CC>merged</color> to form <color=#3366CC>Yemen</color> in 1990.
• <color=#3366CC>Lee Kuan Yew</color> resigned as the prime minister of <color=#3366CC>Singapore</color> on 28 November 1990, a position he had held since
1959, to <color=#3366CC>Goh Chok Tong</color>. Lee remained in the cabinet as Senior Minister.
• In July 1994, <color=#3366CC>North Korean</color> leader <color=#3366CC>Kim Il Sung</color> died, having ruled the country since its founding in 1948. His son
<color=#3366CC>Kim Jong Il</color>, who succeeded him, took over a nation on the brink of complete economic collapse. <color=#3366CC>Famine</color> had
caused a significant number of deaths in the late 1990s, and North Korea gained a reputation for being an
important hub of money laundering, counterfeiting, and weapons proliferation. The country's ability to produce and
sell nuclear weapons became a prominent concern in the international community.
• In 1990, <color=#3366CC>Aung San Suu Kyi</color>'s National League for Democracy in Burma won a majority of seats in the first free
election conducted in 30 years. But the SPDC refused to relinquish power, beginning a peaceful struggle that
began in the 1990s and continued for several decades, primarily fueled by Aung San Suu Kyi and her supporters to
demand the end of military rule.
• Indonesian president <color=#3366CC>Suharto</color> resigned after ruling the country for 32 years (1966–1998), following the riots on
several cities in Indonesia. His resignation marked the beginning of the Reform era.
• In India, the former prime minister <color=#3366CC>Rajiv Gandhi</color> was assassinated on 21 May 1991 by the Tamil Tigers, beginning
a period of economic liberalization led by new prime minister <color=#3366CC>P. V. Narasimha Rao</color>.
• After democratic reforms and steady economic growth in the four Asia-Pacific MNNAs by the United States and
Canada, after the <color=#3366CC>Revolutions of 1989</color>.
• In the <color=#3366CC>Philippines</color>, following the <color=#3366CC>People Power Revolution</color> of 1986 under the <color=#3366CC>Corazon Aquino</color> presidency until 1992,
democratic reforms and economic policies implemented by two Presidents were elected by <color=#3366CC>Fidel V. Ramos</color> in
1992, and Joseph Estrada in 1998.
• South Korea and Taiwan became <color=#3366CC>developed countries</color>, and two of the <color=#3366CC>Four Asian Tigers</color> in the 1990s. Following
democratic reforms in 1988, neoliberal policies were implemented by President <color=#3366CC>Kim Young-sam</color> (South Korea) and
President <color=#3366CC>Lee Teng-hui</color> (Taiwan), both who led their countries during the <color=#3366CC>1997 Asian financial crisis</color>.
• Japan saw eight different prime ministers serve during the 1990s in what was at first called the "Lost Decade" but
later became referred to as the "<color=#3366CC>Lost Decades</color> of the Heisei Era". These included Morihiro Hosokawa, who won the
1993 Japanese general election and formed an opposition coalition until 1996.
Europe
• The improvement in relations between <color=#3366CC>NATO</color> countries and the former members of the <color=#3366CC>Warsaw Pact</color> led to the end
of the <color=#3366CC>Cold War</color>, both in Europe and other parts of the world.
• <color=#3366CC>German reunification</color> – on 3 October 1990, East and West Germany reunified as a result of the collapse of the
<color=#3366CC>Soviet Union</color> and the fall of the <color=#3366CC>Berlin Wall</color>. After reintegrating their economic structure and provincial governments,
Germany focused on the modernization of the formerly communist East. People brought up in socialist East
Germany became integrated with those living in capitalist West Germany.
• <color=#3366CC>Margaret Thatcher</color>, who had been the United Kingdom's prime minister since 1979, resigned as prime minister on
22 November 1990 after being challenged for leadership of the Conservative Party by Michael Heseltine. This was
because of widespread opposition to the introduction of the controversial Community Charge, and the fact that her
key allies such as Nigel Lawson and Geoffrey Howe resigned over the deeply sensitive issues of the <color=#3366CC>Maastricht</color>
<color=#3366CC>Treaty</color> and Thatcher's resistance to Britain joining the European Exchange Rate Mechanism. Less than two years
later, on the infamous Black Wednesday of September 1992, the <color=#3366CC>pound sterling</color> crashed out of the system after the
pound fell below the agreed exchange rate with the Deutsche Mark.
• <color=#3366CC>John Major</color> replaced Thatcher as prime minister in 1990.
• The <color=#3366CC>Perestroika</color> (restructuring) of the Soviet Union destabilized, leading to nationalist and separatist demagogues
gaining popularity. <color=#3366CC>Boris Yeltsin</color>, then chairman of the Supreme Soviet of Russia, resigned from the <color=#3366CC>Communist</color>
<color=#3366CC>Party</color> and became the opposition leader against <color=#3366CC>Mikhail Gorbachev</color>. The Communist Party lost its status as the
governing force of the country and was banned after a <color=#3366CC>coup attempt</color> by communist hardliners attempted to revert
the effects of Gorbachev's policies. Yeltsin's counter-revolution was victorious, and on 25 December 1991,
Gorbachev resigned from the presidency, which led to the <color=#3366CC>dissolution of the Soviet Union</color>. Yeltsin became
president of the Soviet Union's successor, the Russian Federation, and presided over a period of political unrest,
economic crisis, and social anarchy. On 31 December 1999, Yeltsin resigned, leaving <color=#3366CC>Vladimir Putin</color> as acting
president.
• The <color=#3366CC>European Union</color> was formed in 1992 under the <color=#3366CC>Maastricht Treaty</color>.
• The Downing Street Declaration, signed on 15 December 1993 by the prime minister of the United Kingdom, John
Major, and the Taoiseach of Ireland, Albert Reynolds at the British prime minister's office in 10 Downing Street,
affirmed that (1) the right of the people of Ireland to <color=#3366CC>self-determination</color>, and (2) that <color=#3366CC>Northern Ireland</color> would be
transferred to the <color=#3366CC>Republic of Ireland</color> from the United Kingdom only if a majority of its population was in favour of
such a move. It included, as part of the perspective of the so-called "Irish dimension," the principle of consent that
the people of the island of Ireland had the exclusive right to solve the issues between North and South by mutual
consent. The latter statement, which later would become one of the points of the <color=#3366CC>Good Friday Agreement</color>, was key
to producing a positive change of attitude by the Republicans towards a negotiated settlement. The joint
declaration also pledged the governments to seek a peaceful constitutional settlement and promised that parties
linked with paramilitaries (such as Sinn Féin) could take part in the talks so long as they abandoned violence.
• The IRA agreed to a truce in 1994. This marked the beginning of the end of 25 years of violence between the IRA
and the United Kingdom and the start of political negotiations.
• <color=#3366CC>Tony Blair</color> became prime minister in 1997 following a general election.
• The <color=#3366CC>Belfast Agreement</color> (a.k.a. the Good Friday Agreement) was signed by the U.K. and Irish politicians on 10 April
1998, declaring a joint commitment to a peaceful resolution of the territorial dispute between <color=#3366CC>Ireland</color> and the United
Kingdom over <color=#3366CC>Northern Ireland</color>. The 1998 Northern Ireland Good Friday Agreement referendum was held on 22
May 1998, with majority approval.
• The National Assembly for Wales was established following the 1997 Welsh devolution referendum, in which a
majority of voters approved the creation of the National Assembly for Wales.
• In September 1997, the 1997 Scottish devolution referendum was put to the Scottish electorate and secured a
majority in favor of the establishment of a new Scottish Parliament.

Disasters
Natural disasters
The 1990s saw a trend in frequent and more devastating <color=#3366CC>natural disasters</color>, breaking many previous records. Although
the 1990s was designated by the United Nations as an International Decade for Natural Disaster Reduction as part of
its program to prevent losses due to disasters, disasters would go on to cause a record-breaking US$608 billion worth
of damage—more than the past four decades combined.
• The most prominent natural disasters of the decade include: Hurricane Andrew striking South Florida in August
1992, the crippling super storm of March 1993 along the Eastern Seaboard, the devastating 1994 Northridge
earthquake in Los Angeles, the <color=#3366CC>Great Hanshin earthquake</color> in <color=#3366CC>Kobe</color>, Japan in January 1995, the Blizzard of 1996 in
the eastern United States, the US drought of 1999, the deadly Hurricane Mitch which struck Central America in
October 1998, the destructive Oklahoma tornado outbreak in May 1999, the August 1999 İzmit earthquake in
Turkey, and the September 1999 Chi-Chi earthquake in Taiwan.
• A magnitude 7.8 earthquake hit the Philippines on 16 July 1990 and killed around 1000 people in <color=#3366CC>Baguio</color>.
• After 600 years of inactivity, <color=#3366CC>Mount Pinatubo</color> in the <color=#3366CC>Philippines</color> erupted and devastated Zambales and Pampanga in
June 1991.
• July 1995 – Midwestern United States heat wave – An unprecedented heat wave strikes the <color=#3366CC>Midwestern United</color>
<color=#3366CC>States</color> for most of the month. Temperatures peak at 106 °F, and remain above 94 °F in the afternoon for 5 straight
days. At least 739 people died in Chicago alone.
• Hurricane Georges made landfall in at least seven different countries (<color=#3366CC>Antigua and Barbuda</color>, <color=#3366CC>St. Kitts and Nevis</color>,
Haiti, the <color=#3366CC>Dominican Republic</color>, Cuba, the United States and <color=#3366CC>Puerto Rico</color>, a Commonwealth of the United States) –
more than any other hurricane since Hurricane Inez of the 1966 season. The total estimated costs were $60 billion
(about $110 billion in 2022).
• September 1996 – Hurricane Fran made landfall in <color=#3366CC>North Carolina</color>, causing significant damage throughout the
entire state.
• Hurricane Iniki hit the island of <color=#3366CC>Kauai</color> in the Hawaiian Islands on 11 September 1992, making it one of the costliest
hurricanes on record in the eastern Pacific.
• A flood hits the Red River Valley in 1997 becoming the most severe flood since 1826.
• On May 3, 1999, the highest wind speeds recorded on Earth at 321 mph took place during the 1999 Bridge
Creek–Moore tornado outbreak. The estimated costs were $1 billion (about $1.8 billion in 2024). This event was
the first issued tornado emergency by the National Weather Service in history.
• In December 1999, torrential rains and flash floods killed tens of thousands of Venezuelans living in the state of
Vargas in a natural disaster known as the Vargas tragedy.
Non-natural disasters
• Gulf War oil spill: Resulting from actions taken during the <color=#3366CC>Gulf War</color> in 1991 by the Iraq military, the oil spill caused
considerable damage to wildlife in the Persian Gulf, especially in areas surrounding Kuwait and Iraq.
• 11 July 1991: A Nationair Douglas DC-8, chartered by Nigeria Airways, caught fire and crashed in <color=#3366CC>Jeddah, Saudi</color>
<color=#3366CC>Arabia</color>, killing 261 people.

Economics
Many countries, institutions, companies, and organizations were prosperous during the 1990s. High-income countries
such as the United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, Singapore, Hong Kong, Taiwan, South Korea, and
Western Europe experienced steady economic growth for much of the decade during the Great Moderation. However,
in the <color=#3366CC>former Soviet Union</color>, GDP decreased as their economies restructured to produce goods they needed, and some
capital flight occurred.
• In 1993, the <color=#3366CC>General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT)</color> was updated to include the creation of the <color=#3366CC>World</color>
<color=#3366CC>Trade Organization</color>, with the 76 existing GATT members and European Communities becoming the founding
members of the World Trade Organization on 1 January 1995. Opposition by anti-globalization activists showed up
in nearly every GATT summit, like the demonstrations in <color=#3366CC>Seattle</color> in December 1999.
• The anti-globalization protests in the World Trade Organization Ministerial Conference of 1999 in Seattle began on
30 November 1999. This marked the beginning of a steady increase in anti-globalization protests in the first decade
of the 21st century and increasing hostility to <color=#3366CC>neoliberalism</color>.
• U.S. inflation moderated, beginning in 1990 at 5.39%, falling to a low of 1.55% in 1998 and rising slightly to 2.19%
• The <color=#3366CC>G20</color> or Group of Twenty formed on 26 September 1999.
North America
• The decade is seen as a time of great prosperity in the United States and Canada, largely because of the
unexpected advent of the Internet and the explosion of technology industries. The US and Canadian economies
experienced their longest period of peacetime economic expansion, beginning in 1991. Personal incomes doubled
from the recession in 1990, and there was higher productivity overall. The <color=#3366CC>New York Stock Exchange</color> stayed over
the 10,500 mark from 1999 to 2001.
• After the 1992 boom of the US <color=#3366CC>stock market</color>, <color=#3366CC>Alan Greenspan</color> coined the phrase "irrational exuberance", a
reference to the overenthusiasm of investors that typified the trading of this period, and warned of <color=#3366CC>overvaluation</color> of
assets and the stock market generally.
• The <color=#3366CC>North American Free Trade Agreement</color> (NAFTA), which phases out the trade barriers between the United
States, Mexico, and Canada, was signed into law by President <color=#3366CC>Bill Clinton</color>.
Asia
• In the <color=#3366CC>People's Republic of China</color>, the government announced the major <color=#3366CC>privatization</color> of state-owned industries in
September 1997. China entered the 1990s in a turbulent period due to the aftermath of both the <color=#3366CC>Tiananmen</color>
<color=#3366CC>Square Massacre</color> and hardline politicians' efforts to rein in <color=#3366CC>private enterprise</color> and attempt to revive old-fashioned
<color=#3366CC>propaganda</color> campaigns. Relations with the United States deteriorated sharply, and the Chinese leadership was
further embarrassed by the disintegration of <color=#3366CC>communism</color> in Europe. In 1992 <color=#3366CC>Deng Xiaoping</color> <color=#3366CC>travelled</color> to southern
China in his last major public appearance to revitalize faith in <color=#3366CC>market economics</color> and stop the country's slide back
into <color=#3366CC>Maoism</color>. Afterward, China recovered and would experience explosive economic growth during the rest of the
decade. Despite this, dissent continued to be suppressed, and <color=#3366CC>Communist Party</color> General Secretary <color=#3366CC>Jiang Zemin</color>
launched a brutal crackdown against the <color=#3366CC>Falun Gong</color> <color=#3366CC>religious sect</color> in 1999. Deng Xiaoping died in 1997 at the age
of 93. Relations with the US deteriorated again in 1999 after the bombing of the Chinese embassy during the
bombing of Serbia by NATO forces, which caused three deaths, and allegations of Chinese espionage at the Los
Alamos Nuclear Facility.
• <color=#3366CC>Financial crisis</color> hits <color=#3366CC>East</color> and <color=#3366CC>Southeast Asian</color> countries between 1997 and 1998 after a long period of phenomenal
economic development, which continues into 1999. This crisis begins to be felt by the end of the decade.
• In <color=#3366CC>Japan</color>, after three decades of <color=#3366CC>economic growth</color> put them in second place in the world's economies, the county
experienced <color=#3366CC>an economic downturn</color> after 1993. The recession went on into the early first decade of the 21st
century, ending the seemingly unlimited prosperity that the country had previously enjoyed.
• Less affluent nations such as <color=#3366CC>India</color>, <color=#3366CC>Malaysia</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Vietnam</color> also saw tremendous improvements in economic
prosperity and quality of life during the 1990s. Restructuring following the end of the Cold War was beginning.
However, there was also the continuation of terrorism in <color=#3366CC>Third World</color> regions that were once the "frontlines" for
American and Soviet foreign politics, particularly in Asia.
Europe
• By 1990, Soviet leader <color=#3366CC>Mikhail Gorbachev</color>'s reforms were causing major inflation and economic chaos. A <color=#3366CC>coup</color>
attempt by hardliners in August 1991 failed, marking the effective end of the Soviet Union. All its constituent
republics declared their independence by 1991, and Gorbachev resigned from office on Christmas. After 73 years,
the Soviet Union had ceased to exist. The new <color=#3366CC>Russian Federation</color> was headed by <color=#3366CC>Boris Yeltsin</color>, and would face
severe economic difficulty. <color=#3366CC>Oligarchs</color> took over Russia's energy and industrial sectors, reducing almost half the
country to poverty. With a 3% approval rating, Yeltsin had to <color=#3366CC>buy the support of</color> the oligarchs to win reelection in
1996. Economic turmoil and devaluation of the <color=#3366CC>ruble</color> continued, and with <color=#3366CC>heart</color> and <color=#3366CC>alcohol troubles</color>, Yeltsin
stepped down from office on the last day of 1999, handing power to <color=#3366CC>Vladimir Putin</color>.
• <color=#3366CC>Russian financial crisis</color> in the 1990s resulted in mass hyperinflation and prompted economic intervention from the
<color=#3366CC>International Monetary Fund</color> and western countries to help Russia's economy recover.
• The first <color=#3366CC>McDonald's</color> restaurant opened in <color=#3366CC>Moscow</color> in 1990 with then-President of the Supreme Soviet of the
Russian SFSR and future Russian president Boris Yeltsin attending, symbolizing Russia's transition towards a
capitalist <color=#3366CC>free market</color> economy and a move towards adopting elements of <color=#3366CC>Western culture</color>.
• <color=#3366CC>Oil</color> and <color=#3366CC>gas</color> were discovered in many countries in the former Soviet bloc, leading to economic growth and broader
adoption of trade between nations. These trends were also fueled by inexpensive <color=#3366CC>fossil energy</color>, with low <color=#3366CC>petroleum</color>
prices caused by increased oil production. Political stability and decreased militarization due to the winding down of
the <color=#3366CC>Cold War</color> led to economic development and higher living standards for many citizens.
• Most of Europe enjoyed growing prosperity during the 1990s. However, problems including the massive 1995
general strikes in France following a recession and the difficulties associated with <color=#3366CC>German reunification</color> led to
sluggish growth in these countries. However, the French and <color=#3366CC>German</color> economies improved in the latter half of the
decade. Meanwhile, the economies of Spain, <color=#3366CC>Scandinavia</color> and former <color=#3366CC>Eastern Bloc</color> countries accelerated at rapid
speed during the decade. <color=#3366CC>Unemployment rates</color> were low due to many having experienced a deep <color=#3366CC>recession</color> at the
start of the decade.
• After the early 1990s recession, the <color=#3366CC>United Kingdom</color> and Ireland experienced rapid economic growth and falling
unemployment that continued throughout the decade. Economic growth would continue until the <color=#3366CC>Great Recession</color>,
marking the longest uninterrupted period of economic growth in history.

• Some <color=#3366CC>Eastern European</color> economies struggled after the fall of communism, but <color=#3366CC>Poland</color>, <color=#3366CC>Hungary</color>, <color=#3366CC>Czech Republic</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Estonia</color>, <color=#3366CC>Latvia</color> and <color=#3366CC>Lithuania</color> saw economic growth in the late 1990s.
• With the creation of the <color=#3366CC>European Union</color> (EU), there is <color=#3366CC>freedom of movement</color> between member states, such as the
1992 and 1995 free trade agreements.
• The <color=#3366CC>Euro</color> is adopted by the European Union on 1 January 1999, which begins a process of phasing out the former
national currencies of EU countries.
South America
• A Latin American common market, <color=#3366CC>Mercosur</color>, was established in 1991. Mercosur's origins are linked to the
discussions for the constitution of a regional economic market for Latin America, which go back to the treaty that
established the Latin American Free Trade Association in 1960, which was succeeded by the Latin American
Integration Association in the 1980s.
Science and technology
Technology
The 1990s were a revolutionary decade for <color=#3366CC>digital technology</color>. Between 1990 and 1997, household <color=#3366CC>PC</color> ownership in the
US rose from 15% to 35%. Cell phones of the early-1990s and earlier ones were very large, lacked extra features, and
were used by only a few percent of the population of even the advanced nations. Only a few million people used online
services in 1990, and the <color=#3366CC>World Wide Web</color>, which would have a significant impact on technology for many decades,
had only just been invented. The first web browser went online in 1993. By 2001, more than 50% of some Western
countries had Internet access, and more than 25% had cell phone access.
Electronics and communications
Internet
The 90s were a vital period for the development of the <color=#3366CC>Internet</color>. Several inventions and applications were launched to
create the web as it's known today. <color=#3366CC>Tim Berners-Lee</color>, an English computer scientist, released the <color=#3366CC>World Wide Web</color> to
the general public on April 30, 1993. The same year, Mosaic, one of the first widely available web browsers, was
launched as the first browser to display images in line with text and not in a separate window. In 1990, Archie, the
world's first search engine, was released. In the early days of its development, Archie served as an index of <color=#3366CC>File</color>
<color=#3366CC>Transfer Protocol</color> (FTP) sites, which was a method for moving files between a client and a server network. This early
search tool was superseded by more advanced engines like <color=#3366CC>Yahoo!</color> in 1995 and <color=#3366CC>Google</color> in 1998.
Following the launch of the early Internet and fiber optic capabilities to the public, a significant shift occurred.
Consumers, recognizing the potential of the Internet, began to demand more network capacity. This surge in demand
spurred developers to seek solutions to reduce the time and cost of laying new fiber, in order to meet the growing
needs of the public.
In 1992, David Huber, an optical networking engineer, joined forces with entrepreneur Kevin Kimberlin. Together, they
laid the foundation for a new era in telecommunications with the birth of Ciena Corporation. The company would
harness the technology physicist Gordon Gould, inventor of the <color=#3366CC>laser</color> (Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of
Radiation), had pioneered with co-founder William Culver of Optelecom, an early creator of fiber optic cable and optical
amplifiers. Ciena's former <color=#3366CC>chief executive officer</color> Pat Nettles, and a team of engineers attempted to transmit information
on waves of light with a form of a laser. The team began working on a dual-stage optical amplifier that enabled dense
wave division multiplexing (DWDM), which allowed large amounts of data to be transmitted across the nation. The firm
filed a patent on a dual-stage amplifier on November 13, 1995. A year later, in 1996, Ciena made history by deploying
the world's first dense wavelength-division multiplexing (WDM) system on the Sprint fiber network. These
developments eventually formed the backbone of every global communications network, and the foundation of the
Internet.
Prominent <color=#3366CC>websites</color> launched during the decade include <color=#3366CC>IMDb</color> (1993), <color=#3366CC>Amazon</color> (1994), GeoCities (1994), Netscape

(1994), <color=#3366CC>eBay</color> (1995), <color=#3366CC>Yahoo!</color> (1995), AltaVista (1995), ICQ (1996), Hotmail (1996), AIM (1997), <color=#3366CC>Google</color> (1998), <color=#3366CC>Napster</color>
(1999). The pioneering <color=#3366CC>peer-to-peer</color> (P2P) file sharing internet service <color=#3366CC>Napster</color>, which launched in Fall 1999, was the
first peer-to-peer software to become massively popular. While at the time it was possible to share files in other ways
via the Internet (such as <color=#3366CC>IRC</color> and <color=#3366CC>USENET</color>), Napster was the first software to focus exclusively on sharing <color=#3366CC>MP3 files</color> for
<color=#3366CC>music</color>.
• On 6 August 1991, <color=#3366CC>CERN</color>, a pan-European organization for particle research, publicized the new World Wide Web
project. Although the basic applications and guidelines that make the Internet possible had existed for almost two
decades, the network did not gain a public face until the 1990s.
• Advancements in <color=#3366CC>computer modems</color>, ISDN, cable modems, and DSL led to faster connections to the Internet.
• Businesses start to build <color=#3366CC>e-commerce</color> websites; e-commerce-only companies such as <color=#3366CC>Amazon.com</color>, <color=#3366CC>eBay</color>, <color=#3366CC>AOL</color>,
and <color=#3366CC>Yahoo!</color> grow rapidly.
• Driven by mass adoption, consumer <color=#3366CC>personal computer</color> specifications increased dramatically during the 1990s,
from 512 KB RAM 12 MHz Turbo XTs in 1990, to 25–66 MHz 80486-class processor to over 1 GHz CPUs with
close to a gigabyte of RAM by 2000.
• The <color=#3366CC>Year 2000 problem (Y2K)</color> spread fear throughout the United States and eventually the world in the last half of
the decade, particularly in 1999, about possible massive computer malfunctions on 1 January 2000. As a result,
many people stocked up on supplies for fear of a worldwide disaster. After significant effort to upgrade systems on
the part of software engineers, no failures occurred when the clocks rolled over into 2000.
• The first Pentium microprocessor is introduced and developed by the <color=#3366CC>Intel Corporation</color>.
• Email becomes popular; as a result, <color=#3366CC>Microsoft</color> acquires the popular Hotmail webmail service.
• <color=#3366CC>Instant messaging</color> and the buddy list feature becomes popular. AIM and ICQ are two early protocols.
• The introduction of affordable, smaller satellite dishes and the DVB-S standard in the mid-1990s expanded satellite
television services that carried up to 500 television channels.
• The first MP3 player, the MPMan, is released in the late spring of 1998. It came with 32 MB of <color=#3366CC>flash memory</color>
expandable to 64 MB. By the mid-2000s, the MP3 player would overtake the CD player in popularity.
• The first <color=#3366CC>GSM</color> network is launched in Finland in 1991.
• <color=#3366CC>Digital single-lens reflex cameras</color> and regular digital cameras become commercially available. They would replace
film cameras by the late 1990s and early 2000s.
• <color=#3366CC>IBM</color> introduces the 1 in wide Microdrive hard drive in 170 MB and 340 MB capacities.
• <color=#3366CC>Apple Computer</color> in 1998 introduces the iMac all-in-one computer, initiating a trend in computer design towards
translucent plastics and multicolour case design, discontinuing many legacy technologies like serial ports, and
beginning a resurgence in the company's fortunes that continues to this day.
• CD burner drives are introduced.
• The CD-ROM drive became standard for most personal computers during the decade.
• The <color=#3366CC>DVD</color> media format is developed and popularized along with a plethora of <color=#3366CC>Flash memory card</color> standards in
• <color=#3366CC>Pagers</color> are initially popular but ultimately are replaced by mobile phones by the early-2000s.
• Hand-held <color=#3366CC>satellite phones</color> are introduced towards the end of the decade.
• The 24-hour news cycle becomes popular alongside the outbreak of the <color=#3366CC>Gulf War</color> between late 1990 and early
1991, and is solidified with CNN's coverage of <color=#3366CC>Desert Storm</color> and <color=#3366CC>Desert Shield</color>. Though CNN had been running
24-hour newscasts since 1980, it was not until the Gulf War that the general public took notice, and others imitated
CNN's non-stop news approach.
• <color=#3366CC>Portable CD players</color>, introduced during the late 1980s, became very popular and profoundly impacted the music
industry and youth culture during the 1990s.
• In 1992, <color=#3366CC>Fujitsu</color> introduced the world's first 21 in full-color display <color=#3366CC>plasma display</color> television set.
Software
• <color=#3366CC>Microsoft Windows</color> operating systems become virtually ubiquitous on <color=#3366CC>IBM PC compatibles</color>.
• <color=#3366CC>Microsoft</color> introduces <color=#3366CC>Windows 3.1</color>, Windows 95, and Windows 98 to the market, which gain immediate popularity.
• Macintosh System 7 was released in 1991. For much of the decade, Apple would struggle to develop a
next-generation graphical operating system, starting with Copland and culminating in its December 1996 buyout of
NeXT and the 1999 release of Mac OS X Server 1.0.
• The development of <color=#3366CC>web browsers</color> such as Netscape Navigator and <color=#3366CC>Internet Explorer</color> makes surfing the <color=#3366CC>World</color>
<color=#3366CC>Wide Web</color> easier and more user-friendly.
• The <color=#3366CC>Java programming language</color> is developed by Sun Microsystems (later acquired by <color=#3366CC>Oracle</color> in 2009–2010).
• In 1991, development of the free Linux kernel was started by 21-year-old <color=#3366CC>Linus Torvalds</color> in Finland.
• SolidWorks <color=#3366CC>computer-aided design</color> software for Windows released in 1995.
• Macromedia Shockwave Player for multimedia in browsers released in 1995.
• Winamp media player first released 1997.
• QuickTime media player created in 1991.
Rail transportation
The opening of the <color=#3366CC>Channel Tunnel</color> between France and the United Kingdom saw the commencement by the three
national railway companies of Belgium, France, and the United Kingdom, respectively SNCB/NMBS, <color=#3366CC>SNCF</color> and British
Rail of the joint <color=#3366CC>Eurostar</color> service.
On 14 November 1994 Eurostar services began between Waterloo International station in London, Gare du Nord in
Paris and Brussels South in Brussels. In 1995 Eurostar was achieving an average end-to-end speed of 171.5 km/h
between London and Paris. On 8 January 1996 Eurostar launched services from a second railway station in the UK
when Ashford International was opened. Journey times between London and Brussels were reduced by the opening of
the High Speed 1 line on 14 December 1997.
Automobiles
The 1990s began with a <color=#3366CC>recession</color> that dampened car sales. <color=#3366CC>General Motors</color> suffered huge losses because of an
inefficient structure, stale designs, and poor quality. Sales improved with the economy by the mid-1990s, but GM's US
market share gradually declined to less than 40% (from a peak of 50% in the 1970s). While the new Saturn division
fared well, Oldsmobile fell sharply, and attempts to remake the division as a European-style luxury car were
unsuccessful.
Cars in the 1990s had a rounder, more streamlined shape than those from the 1970s and 1980s; this style would
continue early into the 2000s and to a lesser extent later on.
<color=#3366CC>Chrysler</color> ran into financial troubles as it entered the 1990s. Like GM, the Chrysler too had a stale model lineup (except
for the best-selling minivans) that were largely based on the aging K-car platform. In 1992, chairman <color=#3366CC>Lee Iacocca</color>
retired, and the company began a remarkable revival, introducing the new LH platform and "Cab-Forward" styling,
along with a highly successful redesign of the full-sized Dodge Ram in 1994. Chrysler's minivans continued to dominate
the market despite increasing competition. In 1998, Daimler-Benz (the parent company of <color=#3366CC>Mercedes-Benz</color>) merged
with Chrysler. The following year, it was decided to retire Plymouth, which had been on a long decline since the 1970s.
<color=#3366CC>Ford</color> continued to fare well in the 1990s, with the second and third generations of the Ford Taurus being named the
best-selling car in the United States from 1992 to 1996. However, the Taurus would be outsold and dethroned by the
Toyota Camry starting in 1997, which became the best-selling car in the United States for the rest of the decade and
into the 2000s. Ford also introduced the Ford Explorer, with the first model being sold in 1991. Ford's Explorer became
the best-selling SUV on the market, outselling both the Chevy Blazer and Jeep Cherokee.
Japanese cars continued to be highly successful during the decade. The Honda Accord vied with the Taurus most
years for being the best-selling car in the United States during the early decade. Although launched in 1989, the luxury
brands Lexus and Infiniti began car sales of 1990 model year vehicles and saw great success. Lexus would go on to
outsell Mercedes-Benz and BMW in the United States by 1991 and outsell Cadillac and Lincoln by the end of the
decade. SUVs and trucks became hugely popular during the economic boom in the decade's second half. Many
manufacturers that had never built a truck before started selling SUVs. Fabrication during the 1990s became gradually
rounder and ovoid, the Ford Taurus and Mercury Sable being some of the more extreme examples. Safety features
such as <color=#3366CC>airbags</color> and shoulder belts became mandatory equipment on new cars.
Science
• Physicists develop <color=#3366CC>M-theory</color>.
• Detection of <color=#3366CC>extrasolar planets</color> orbiting <color=#3366CC>stars</color> other than the Sun.
• In the United Kingdom, the first <color=#3366CC>cloned</color> mammal, <color=#3366CC>Dolly the sheep</color> was confirmed by the Roslin Institute, and was
reported by global media on 26 February 1997. Dolly would trigger a raging controversy on cloning, and <color=#3366CC>bioethical</color>
concerns regarding possible human cloning continue to this day.
• The NIH launched the <color=#3366CC>Human Genome Project</color> in 1990 under the leadership of <color=#3366CC>Francis Collins</color>, with the goal of
sequencing the entire human genome. In the same year, Mary-Claire King's discovery of the link between heritable
breast cancers and a gene found on chromosome 17q21 sparked a wave of collaborative research. Inspired by this
breakthrough, scientists Mark Skolnick and Walter Gilbert, in partnership with entrepreneur Kevin Kimberlin, joined
forces to establish Myriad Genetics, a company dedicated to sequencing the BRCA1 gene. In 1991, Skolnick and
his team of scientists developed a gene mapping method, Restriction Fragment-length Polymorphisms (RFLP), to
help locate the cancer gene. The company later introduced the first commercial genetic test for assessing the risk
of hereditary breast and ovarian cancer, the BRACAnalysis. The Human Genome Project was partially completed
in 2003 with a 92% accuracy. It was not until 2022 that the final complete human genome sequence was published.
• <color=#3366CC>DNA</color> identification of individuals finds wide application in <color=#3366CC>criminal law</color>. Brazil, United States, United Kingdom,
Russia and The Netherlands established their own national DNA database.
• <color=#3366CC>Hubble Space Telescope</color> was launched in 1990 and revolutionized <color=#3366CC>astronomy</color>. Unfortunately, a flaw in its main
mirror caused it to produce fuzzy, distorted images. This was corrected by a <color=#3366CC>Space Shuttle</color> repair mission in 1993.
• Protease inhibitors introduced, allowing HAART therapy against HIV; drastically reduces AIDS mortality.
• <color=#3366CC>NASA</color>'s spacecraft Pathfinder lands on <color=#3366CC>Mars</color> and deploys a small roving vehicle, Sojourner, which analyzes the
planet's geology and atmosphere.
• The <color=#3366CC>Hale–Bopp</color> comet swings past the Sun for the first time in 4,200 years in April 1997.
• Development of <color=#3366CC>biodegradable products</color>, replacing products made from <color=#3366CC>polystyrene foam</color>; advances in methods for
<color=#3366CC>recycling</color> of waste products (such as paper, glass, and aluminum).
• Genetically engineered crops are developed for commercial use.
• Discovery of <color=#3366CC>dark matter</color>, <color=#3366CC>dark energy</color>, <color=#3366CC>brown dwarfs</color>, and first confirmation of <color=#3366CC>black holes</color>.
• The Galileo probe orbits <color=#3366CC>Jupiter</color>, studying the planet and its moons extensively.
• <color=#3366CC>Comet Shoemaker–Levy 9</color> (formally designated D/1993 F2, nicknamed String of Pearls for its appearance) was a
comet that broke apart and collided with Jupiter in July 1994, providing the first direct observation of an
extraterrestrial collision of Solar System objects.
• The <color=#3366CC>Global Positioning System</color> (GPS) becomes fully operational.
• Proof of <color=#3366CC>Fermat's Last Theorem</color> is discovered by <color=#3366CC>Andrew Wiles</color>.
• Construction started in 1998 on the <color=#3366CC>International Space Station</color>.
Society
The 1990s represented continuing social liberalization in most countries, coupled with an increase in the influence of
capitalism, which would continue until the <color=#3366CC>Great Recession</color> of the late 2000s/early 2010s.
• <color=#3366CC>Youth culture</color> in the 1990s responded to this by embracing both environmentalism and <color=#3366CC>entrepreneurship</color>. Fashion
of the Western world reflected this by often turning highly <color=#3366CC>individualistic</color> and/or <color=#3366CC>counter-cultural</color>, which was

influenced by <color=#3366CC>Generation X</color> and early <color=#3366CC>millennials</color>: <color=#3366CC>tattoos</color> and <color=#3366CC>body piercings</color> gained popularity, and "retro" styles,
inspired by fashions of the 1960s and 1970s, were also prevalent. Some young people became increasingly
involved in <color=#3366CC>extreme sports</color> and outdoor activities that combined embracing athletics with the appreciation of nature.
• In 1990 the <color=#3366CC>World Health Organization</color> removed homosexuality from its list of diseases. Increasing acceptance of
openly homosexual people occurred in the western world, slowly starting in the early 1990s. Biphobia towards
bisexual men became somewhat fashionable amongst heterosexual women and gay men, while lesbians and
bisexual women complained of being commodified by publishing and film industries to cater to heterosexual men.
• Following the murder of actress Rebecca Schaeffer by a <color=#3366CC>stalker</color>, America's first anti-stalking laws, including
California Penal Code 646.9 were passed in 1990. California also passed the first cyberstalking law in 1999
(§646.9 of the California Penal Code).

Portugal, November 1994.

cases.

Environment
At the beginning of the decade, <color=#3366CC>sustainable development</color> and <color=#3366CC>environmental protection</color> became serious issues for
governments and the international community. In 1987, the publication of the Brundtland Report by the United Nations
paved the way to establish an environmental governance. In 1992, the Earth Summit was held in <color=#3366CC>Rio de Janeiro</color>, in
which several countries committed to protect the environment, signing a Convention on Biological Diversity.
The prevention of the destruction of the <color=#3366CC>tropical rainforests</color> of the world is a major environmental cause that first came
into wide public concern in the early 1990s and has continued and accelerated in its prominence.
The <color=#3366CC>Chernobyl disaster</color> had significant impact on public opinion at the end of the 1980s, and the fallout was still
causing cancer deaths well into the 1990s and possibly even into the 21st century. Well into the 1990s, several
environmental NGOs helped improve <color=#3366CC>environmental awareness</color> among public opinion and governments. The most
famous of these organizations during this decade was <color=#3366CC>Greenpeace</color>, which did not hesitate to lead illegal actions in the
name of environmental preservation. These organizations also drew attention to the <color=#3366CC>large deforestation</color> of the <color=#3366CC>Amazon</color>
<color=#3366CC>rainforest</color> during the period.
<color=#3366CC>Global warming</color> as an aspect of <color=#3366CC>climate change</color> also became a major concern, and the creation of the United Nations
Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) after the Earth Summit helped coordinate efforts to reduce
carbon emissions in the atmosphere. From 1995, the UNFCCC held annual summits on climate change, leading to the
adoption of the <color=#3366CC>Kyoto Protocol</color> in December 1997, a binding agreement signed by several developed countries.
The 1989 <color=#3366CC>EPA</color> total ban on <color=#3366CC>asbestos</color> was overturned in 1991.
In 1996, (Anderson, et al. v. Pacific Gas & Electric, file BCV 00300) alleged contamination of drinking water with
hexavalent chromium and the case was settled for (US) $333 million, a new record for a direct-action lawsuit.
Third-wave feminism

• <color=#3366CC>Anita Hill</color> and other women testify before the <color=#3366CC>United States Congress</color> on being <color=#3366CC>sexually harassed</color> by <color=#3366CC>Supreme</color>
<color=#3366CC>Court</color> nominee Clarence Thomas. Thomas was narrowly confirmed by the <color=#3366CC>United States Senate</color>, but Hill's
testimony, and the testimony of other harassed women, begins a national debate on the issue.
• Record numbers of women are elected to high office in the United States in 1992, the "Year of the Woman".
• <color=#3366CC>Violence against women</color> takes centre stage as an essential issue internationally. The Violence Against Women Act
was passed in the United States, which greatly affected the world community through the United Nations. The law's
author, <color=#3366CC>Joe Biden</color>, UN Ambassador and Secretary of State <color=#3366CC>Madeleine Albright</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Hillary Clinton</color> (see below)
have become vocal advocates of action against violence against women.
• Women reach great heights of power in the United States government. Hillary Clinton, leading policy proposals,
traveling abroad as a State Department representative to 82 nations, advising her husband, and being elected a
<color=#3366CC>senator</color> (in 2000), is the most openly empowered and politically powerful first lady in American history; Madeleine
Albright and Janet Reno take two of the cabinet's top jobs as United States Secretary of State (#1), and United
States Attorney General (#4), respectively. Sheila Widnall becomes head and Secretary of the Air Force, and <color=#3366CC>Ruth</color>
<color=#3366CC>Bader Ginsburg</color> joins <color=#3366CC>Sandra Day O'Connor</color> as the second woman on the <color=#3366CC>U.S. Supreme Court</color>.
• More nations than ever before are led by elected women Presidents and Prime Ministers. Prime Minister <color=#3366CC>Benazir</color>
<color=#3366CC>Bhutto</color>'s 1988 victory in Pakistan makes great strides for women leaders in Muslim states. In Turkey, <color=#3366CC>Tansu Çiller</color>
became the first female prime minister in 1993.
• In popular culture, British pop group the <color=#3366CC>Spice Girls</color> also played a part in the feminist movement, boosting
popularity with their slogan "Girl Power!", while country music superstar <color=#3366CC>Shania Twain</color> declared female supremacy
in her 1995 hit song "Any Man of Mine."
Baby boomers
Marketing campaigns aimed at young adults in wealthy English-Speaking Countries were informed by unscientific
theories about selling to so-called <color=#3366CC>Generation X</color> and <color=#3366CC>Baby boomers</color>. Few people embraced the labels Generation X and
Baby Boomer as self-descriptors. Films with characters depicting the Generation X stereotype included Slacker (1990),
The Brady Bunch Movie (1995) and Austin Powers.

Europe

when their chauffeured, hired Mercedes-Benz S-Class crashed in the Pont de l'Alma tunnel. The chauffeur, Henri
Paul, died at the scene, as did Al-Fayed. Diana and an Al-Fayed bodyguard, Trevor Rees-Jones, survived the
accident. The Princess of Wales died at a Paris hospital hours later. The bodyguard, Rees-Jones, is the sole

tunnel in the world.

succession to the position.
North America
• <color=#3366CC>Eric Harris and Dylan Klebold</color> kill 14 people and then themselves during the <color=#3366CC>Columbine High School shooting</color> in
April 1999, which would inspire a number of future <color=#3366CC>school shooters</color> to commit similar offenses.
• O. J. Simpson murder case – <color=#3366CC>O. J. Simpson</color>'s trial, described in the American media as the "trial of the century",
proceeds for nearly a year under intense media publicity. A majority of the trial was broadcast nightly during prime
time television. On 3 October 1995, Simpson was found not guilty of the double-murder of ex-wife Nicole Brown
Simpson and her friend, Ronald Goldman.
• With help from clinical fertility drugs, an Iowa mother, Bobbie McCaughey, gave birth to the first surviving
<color=#3366CC>septuplets</color> in 1997. There followed a media frenzy and widespread support for the family.
• John F. Kennedy Jr., his wife Carolyn Bessette and sister-in-law Lauren Bessette are killed when Kennedy's private
plane crashes off the coast of Martha's Vineyard in July 1999.
• Debate on assisted suicide, highly publicized by <color=#3366CC>Michigan</color> doctor <color=#3366CC>Jack Kevorkian</color>, surfaces when Kevorkian is
charged with multiple counts of <color=#3366CC>homicide</color> of his terminally ill patients through the decade.
• Beer keg registration becomes a popular public policy in the United States.
• The 500th anniversary of <color=#3366CC>Christopher Columbus'</color> purported discovery of the Americas in 1992 was popularly
observed in the United States, despite controversy and protests against the victimization of Native Americans by
Columbus' expeditions. The holiday was labeled by some as <color=#3366CC>racist</color>, in view of Native American experiences of
<color=#3366CC>colonialism</color>, <color=#3366CC>slavery</color>, <color=#3366CC>genocide</color>, and cultural destruction.
• <color=#3366CC>Matthew Shepard</color> is murdered near the University of Wyoming, purportedly for being <color=#3366CC>gay</color>. This sparks intense
national and international media attention and outrage. Shepard becomes a major symbol in the <color=#3366CC>LGBT</color> rights
movement and the fight against <color=#3366CC>homophobia</color>. Claims of crystal methamphetamine related "meth rage" as a
contributing factor in the crime surfaced in 2013.
• Shanda Sharer was murdered on 11 January 1992. She was lured away from her house and held captive by a
group of teenage girls. She was tortured for hours and burned alive. She died from smoke inhalation. Those found
guilty and sentenced to prison were Melinda Loveless, Laurie Tackett, Hope Rippey, and Toni Lawrence.
According to Loveless, she was jealous of her former partner Amanda Heavrin's relationship with Shanda Sharer.
• Karla Homolka was arrested with her husband, Paul Bernardo, in 1993. Both sexually tortured and killed their
victims. Their first victim was Karla's 15-year-old sister, Tammy Homolka. The second and third victims were Leslie
Mahaffy and Kristen French. Karla told the investigators that she reluctantly did what Paul told her to do because
he was abusive, and was given a plea deal. She was sentenced to 12 years in prison (10 years for Mahaffy and
French, and two years for Tammy). Later, investigators discovered the crime videotapes, proving that Karla was a
willing participant. But by that time the deal had already been made. In 1995, Paul was sentenced to life in prison.
Karla was released from prison in 2005.
• Polly Klaas (3 January 1981 – October 1993) was kidnapped by Richard Allen Davis from her home during a
slumber party. She was later strangled to death. After her death, her father, Marc Klaas, established the KlaasKids
Foundation.
• Jonbenet Ramsey (6 August 1990 – 25 December 1996) was a child beauty pageant contestant who was missing
and found dead in her Boulder, Colorado, home. The crime terrified the nation and the world. Her parents were
initially considered to be suspects in her death but were cleared in 2003 when DNA from her clothes was tested. To
this day, her murderer has not been found and brought to justice.
• Lorena Bobbitt was charged with malicious wounding for severing her husband John Bobbitt's penis after she was
repeatedly sexually assaulted by Bobbitt, for which he was charged. Both parties were acquitted of their respective
crimes. The story was notable because of the use of Microsurgery to re-attach the man's penis.
• Wanda Holloway was convicted of solicitation of capital murder when she attempted to hire a <color=#3366CC>hitman</color> to kill the
mother of her daughter's junior high school cheerleading rival.
• American singer-songwriter, guitarist, and actor <color=#3366CC>John Denver</color> died in a plane crash in Monterey Bay near Pacific
Grove on 12 October 1997.
• Scandal rocked the sport of <color=#3366CC>figure skating</color> when skater Nancy Kerrigan was attacked during practice by an
assailant hired by Jeff Gillooly, former husband of skater Tonya Harding. The attack was carried out in an attempt
to injure Kerrigan's leg to the point of her being unable to compete in the upcoming 1994 Winter Olympics, thereby
securing Harding a better spot to win a <color=#3366CC>gold medal</color>.
• <color=#3366CC>1992 Los Angeles riots</color> – resulted in 53 deaths and 5,500 property fires in a 100 sqmi riot zone. The riots were a
result of the state court <color=#3366CC>acquittal</color> of three white and one Hispanic L.A. police officer by an all-white jury in a police
brutality case involving motorist <color=#3366CC>Rodney King</color>. In 1993, all four officers were convicted in a federal civil rights case.

Asia

Popular culture
Film
Live-action films
Dogme 95 became an important European artistic motion picture movement by the decade's end. Also in 1998, <color=#3366CC>Titanic</color>
by director <color=#3366CC>James Cameron</color> (released in late 1997) became the highest-grossing film of all time, grossing over $1.8
billion worldwide. It would hold this record for over a decade until 2010 when James Cameron's <color=#3366CC>Avatar</color> (released in
December 2009), took the title.
<color=#3366CC>Crime films</color> were also extremely popular during the 1990s and garnered several awards throughout the decade, such
as <color=#3366CC>Goodfellas</color>, <color=#3366CC>Pulp Fiction</color>, L.A. Confidential, <color=#3366CC>Heat</color>, Boyz n the Hood, Se7en, Thelma & Louise, Fargo, A Simple Plan,
and many others. Live-action films featuring computer-animated characters became popular, with films such as Casper,
101 Dalmatians, Men in Black and Stuart Little proving financially successful. Live-action/traditional cel animated film
featuring traditional characters like Space Jam, Cool World, and The Pagemaster were prevalent as well.
In Argentina, a new artistic movement appeared in the filmmaking scene, called, which would be greatly influential in
Latin American cinema.
Animated films
In 1994, former Disney employee Jeffrey Katzenberg founded DreamWorks SKG, which would produce its first two
animated films: The Prince of Egypt and Antz which were both aimed more at adults than children and were both
critically and commercially successful. <color=#3366CC>Toy Story</color>, the first full-length <color=#3366CC>CGI</color> movie, made by <color=#3366CC>Pixar</color>, was released in 1995
and revolutionized animated films. In 1998, with the release of DreamWorks's Antz and Pixar's A Bug's Life, the rivalry
between DreamWorks and Pixar began between the studios due to the similarities between both films.
Meanwhile, films by Pixar's parent company, <color=#3366CC>Disney</color> became popular once more when the studio returned to making
family-oriented animated musical films. Disney Animation was navigating the "<color=#3366CC>Disney Renaissance</color>", through both
animated theatrical films and animated television series on the <color=#3366CC>Disney Channel</color> (owned by Walt Disney Television). The
"Disney Renaissance" began with The Little Mermaid in 1989 and ended with Tarzan in 1999. Films of this era include
<color=#3366CC>Beauty and the Beast</color>, Aladdin, The Nightmare Before Christmas, <color=#3366CC>The Lion King</color>, Pocahontas, The Hunchback of Notre
Dame, Hercules, and Mulan.
Japanese <color=#3366CC>anime</color> films remained popular throughout the 1990s with the release of <color=#3366CC>Studio Ghibli</color> films such as Only
Yesterday, Porco Rosso, Pom Poko, Whisper of the Heart, <color=#3366CC>Princess Mononoke</color> (which became the highest-grossing
anime film at the time) and My Neighbors the Yamadas. Other significant anime films which gained cult status include
Roujin Z, Ramayana: The Legend of Prince Rama, Patlabor 2: The Movie, Ninja Scroll, Street Fighter II: The Animated
Movie, Ghost in the Shell, Memories, The End of Evangelion, Perfect Blue, and.
The British stop-motion animated film series <color=#3366CC>Wallace & Gromit</color>, which started in 1989 with A Grand Day Out, became a
cultural phenomenon in this decade, and now has been expanded with over four short films and two feature-length
films.
Other significant animated films have also gained cult status, such as The Iron Giant, Batman: Mask of the Phantasm,
A Goofy Movie, Cats Don't Dance, All Dogs Go to Heaven 2, Wakko's Wish, Ferngully: The Last Rainforest, Anastasia,
and Kirikou and the Sorceress.

Music
Music artists and genres
Music marketing became more segmented in the 1990s, as <color=#3366CC>MTV</color> gradually shifted away from music videos and radio
splintered into narrower formats aimed at various niches. However, the 1990s are perhaps best known for <color=#3366CC>grunge</color>,

<color=#3366CC>gangsta rap</color>, <color=#3366CC>R&B</color>, teen pop; Eurodance, <color=#3366CC>electronic dance music</color>, the renewed popularity of <color=#3366CC>punk rock</color> from the band
<color=#3366CC>Green Day</color> and their 1994 album Dookie (which would also help create a new genre <color=#3366CC>pop-punk</color>), and for the entrance of
<color=#3366CC>alternative rock</color> into the mainstream. <color=#3366CC>U2</color> was one of the most popular 1990s bands; their groundbreaking Zoo TV and
PopMart tours were the top-selling tours of 1992 and 1997, respectively. <color=#3366CC>Glam metal</color> died out in the music mainstream

by 1991. <color=#3366CC>Grunge</color> became popular in the early 1990s due to the success of <color=#3366CC>Nirvana</color>'s <color=#3366CC>Nevermind</color>, <color=#3366CC>Pearl Jam</color>'s Ten, <color=#3366CC>Alice</color>
<color=#3366CC>in Chains</color>' Dirt, Soundgarden's Badmotorfinger and Stone Temple Pilots' Core. <color=#3366CC>pop-punk</color> also becomes popular with
such artists as Green Day, <color=#3366CC>Blink-182</color>, <color=#3366CC>Weezer</color>, Social Distortion, the Offspring, Bad Religion, NOFX and Rancid. Other
successful alternative acts included <color=#3366CC>Red Hot Chili Peppers</color>, <color=#3366CC>R.E.M.</color>, Nickelback, Creed, <color=#3366CC>Radiohead</color>, Gin Blossoms, Soul
Asylum, Goo Goo Dolls, Third Eye Blind, Faith No More, <color=#3366CC>the Smashing Pumpkins</color>, Live, Everclear, Bush, Screaming
Trees and Ween.
Rappers <color=#3366CC>Salt-n-Pepa</color> continued to have hit songs until 1994. <color=#3366CC>Dr. Dre</color>'s 1992 album <color=#3366CC>The Chronic</color> provided a template for
modern <color=#3366CC>gangsta rap</color>, and gave rise to other emerging artists of the genre, including <color=#3366CC>Snoop Dogg</color>. Due to the success of
Death Row Records and Tupac Shakur, West Coast gangsta rap commercially dominated hip-hop during the
early-to-mid 1990s, along with Bad Boy Records and the Notorious B.I.G. on the East Coast. Hip-hop became the
best-selling music genre by the mid-1990s.
1994 became a breakthrough year for punk rock in California, with the success of bands like Bad Religion, Social
Distortion, <color=#3366CC>Blink-182</color>, <color=#3366CC>Green Day</color>, the Offspring, Rancid and similar groups following. This success would continue to
grow over the next decade. The 1990s also became the most important decade for ska punk/reggae rock, with the
success of many bands like Smash Mouth, Buck-O-Nine, Goldfinger, Less Than Jake, the Mighty Mighty Bosstones,
Murphy's Law, No Doubt, Reel Big Fish, Save Ferris, Sublime and Sugar Ray.
The <color=#3366CC>rave</color> movement that emerged in the late 1980s continued to grow in popularity. This movement spawned genres
such as Intelligent dance music and <color=#3366CC>Drum and bass</color>. The latter is an offshoot of jungle techno and breakbeat. Popular
artists included <color=#3366CC>Moby</color>, Fatboy Slim, <color=#3366CC>Björk</color>, <color=#3366CC>Aphex Twin</color>, Orbital, the Orb, the Chemical Brothers, Basement Jaxx, Todd
Terry, 808 State, Primal Scream, the Shamen, the KLF and <color=#3366CC>the Prodigy</color>.
The rise of <color=#3366CC>industrial music</color>, somewhat a fusion of <color=#3366CC>synthpop</color> and <color=#3366CC>heavy metal</color>, rose to worldwide popularity with bands
like Godflesh, <color=#3366CC>Nine Inch Nails</color>, <color=#3366CC>Rammstein</color>, Ministry and <color=#3366CC>Marilyn Manson</color>. Groove metal was born through the efforts of
<color=#3366CC>Pantera</color>, whose seventh studio album Far Beyond Driven (1994) was notable for going number one on Billboard 200.
Another heavy metal subgenre called nu metal, which mixed metal with hip-hop influences, became popular with bands
like <color=#3366CC>Korn</color>, Slipknot and Limp Bizkit selling millions of albums worldwide. <color=#3366CC>Metallica</color>'s 1991 eponymous album <color=#3366CC>Metallica</color> is
the best-selling album of the SoundScan era, while extreme metal acts such as <color=#3366CC>Death</color>, <color=#3366CC>Mayhem</color>, Darkthrone, Emperor,
Cannibal Corpse and others experienced popularity throughout the decade.
The theatrical traveling Irish dance troupe Riverdance was first performed as a seven-minute interval act for the 1994
Eurovision Song Contest in Dublin, originally led by <color=#3366CC>Michael Flatley</color> and Jean Butler, to a thunderous ovation. The
following year, it quickly evolved into one of the most successful full-fledged stage shows in history.
Country music
In the 1990s, country music became a worldwide phenomenon thanks to Billy Ray Cyrus, <color=#3366CC>Shania Twain</color> and <color=#3366CC>Garth</color>
<color=#3366CC>Brooks</color>. The latter enjoyed one of the most successful careers in popular music history, breaking records for both sales
and concert attendance throughout the decade. The RIAA has certified his recordings at a combined (128× platinum),
denoting roughly 113 million United States shipments.
Other artists that experienced success during this time included Clint Black, Sammy Kershaw, Aaron Tippin, Travis
Tritt, Suzy Bogguss, Alan Jackson, Lorrie Morgan and the newly formed duo of Brooks & Dunn. <color=#3366CC>George Strait</color>, whose
career began in the 1980s, also continued to have widespread success in this decade and beyond. Female artists such
as Reba McEntire, <color=#3366CC>Faith Hill</color>, Martina McBride, Deana Carter, LeAnn Rimes and Mary Chapin Carpenter all released
platinum-selling albums in the 1990s. Rimes, a teenager at the time, spawned a "teen movement" in country music;
with fellow teen artists Lila McCann, Jessica Andrews, Billy Gillman, and others following suit; a phenomenon that
hasn't been duplicated since Tanya Tucker and Marie Osmond in the early 1970s. The <color=#3366CC>Dixie Chicks</color> became one of the
most popular country bands in the 1990s and early 2000s. Their 1998 debut album Wide Open Spaces went on to
become certified 12× platinum, while their 1999 album Fly went on to become 10× platinum.
R&B and related
Contemporary quiet storm and <color=#3366CC>R&B</color> continued to be quite popular among adult audiences originating from
African-American communities, which began during the 1980s. Popular African-American contemporary R&B artists

included <color=#3366CC>Mariah Carey</color>, <color=#3366CC>D'Angelo</color>, <color=#3366CC>Lauryn Hill</color>, <color=#3366CC>Whitney Houston</color>, Brandy, En Vogue, <color=#3366CC>TLC</color>, <color=#3366CC>Destiny's Child</color>, <color=#3366CC>Toni Braxton</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Boyz II Men</color>, Dru Hill, Vanessa Williams and <color=#3366CC>Janet Jackson</color>.
Also, British R&B artists Sade (active since 1982), Des'Ree and Mark Morrison became quite popular during this
decade.
Music from around the world
In the <color=#3366CC>United Kingdom</color>, the alternative rock <color=#3366CC>Britpop</color> genre emerged as part of the more general Cool Britannia culture,
with Pulp (already founded in 1978), <color=#3366CC>Blur</color> (active since 1988), Ocean Colour Scene (since 1989), Suede (existing since
1989 with hiatus), the Verve (1990–1993), <color=#3366CC>Oasis</color> (formed in 1991), Elastica (1992–2001), Ash (since 1992), Supergrass
(1993–2022 with hiatus) and Kula Shaker (since 1995) serving as popular examples of this emergence.
The impact of boy band pop sensation <color=#3366CC>Take That</color>, founded in 1990, lead to the formation of other boy bands in the UK
and Ireland, such as East 17 in 1991 and the Irish boy band Boyzone in 1993. Female pop icons <color=#3366CC>Spice Girls</color> took the
world by storm since 1994, becoming the most commercially successful British group since <color=#3366CC>the Beatles</color>, <color=#3366CC>the Rolling</color>
<color=#3366CC>Stones</color> and <color=#3366CC>Led Zeppelin</color>. Their global success brought about a widespread scene of teen pop acts around the world
such as All Saints, <color=#3366CC>Backstreet Boys</color> (both formed in 1993) as well as American acts as Hanson (from 1992), <color=#3366CC>NSYNC</color>
(1995–2002, reunited 2003), <color=#3366CC>Britney Spears</color> and <color=#3366CC>Christina Aguilera</color> who came to prominence into the new millennium.
Many musicians from Canada, such as <color=#3366CC>Celine Dion</color>, Maestro Fresh Wes, Snow, Barenaked Ladies, <color=#3366CC>Shania Twain</color>, Len,
Sarah McLachlan, and <color=#3366CC>Alanis Morissette</color> became known worldwide.
Argentine rock music continues to be commercially successful and culturally relevant throughout the 1990s. <color=#3366CC>Soda</color>
<color=#3366CC>Stereo</color>, the most famous rock band of Latin America reached new heights with their album Canción Animal in 1990,
which contained great anthems of Argentine Rock, such as De Música Ligera, Té para tres and Entre Caníbales. Many
bands of the Underground scene become mainstream, such as <color=#3366CC>hard rock</color> band, La Renga, <color=#3366CC>post-punk</color> band Los
Redondos and <color=#3366CC>alternative rock</color> band Babasónicos. Also <color=#3366CC>Charly García</color> and Fito Páez would continue their successful
solo careers, the latter with one of hist most famous albums, Circo Beat, and his classic song,.
In 1991, Australian children's music group <color=#3366CC>The Wiggles</color> appeared.
In Japan, the <color=#3366CC>J-pop</color> genre emerged as part of the more general Heisei Power cultural movement, with <color=#3366CC>B'z</color>, <color=#3366CC>Mr. Children</color>,

<color=#3366CC>Southern All Stars</color>, Yumi Matsutoya, Dreams Come True, Glay, Zard, <color=#3366CC>Hikaru Utada</color>, <color=#3366CC>Namie Amuro</color>, <color=#3366CC>SMAP</color>, Chage and

Speed, Wands, and Field of View became more popular for Japanese youth audiences during the <color=#3366CC>Lost Decades</color>.
The Tibetan Freedom Concert, organized by <color=#3366CC>Beastie Boys</color> and the Milarepa Fund, brought 120,000 people together in
the interest of increased human rights and autonomy for <color=#3366CC>Tibet</color> from China.
Controversies
Controversy surrounded <color=#3366CC>the Prodigy</color> with the release of the track "Smack My Bitch Up". The National Organization for
Women (NOW) claimed that the track was "advocating violence against women" due to the song's lyrics, which are
themselves sampled from Ultramagnetic MCs' "Give the Drummer Some". The music video (directed by Jonas
Åkerlund) featured a first-person POV of someone going clubbing, indulging in drugs and alcohol, getting into fist fights,
abusing women and picking up a prostitute. At the end of the video, the camera pans over to a mirror, revealing the
subject to be a woman.
Deaths of artists
1991 also saw the death of <color=#3366CC>Queen</color> frontman <color=#3366CC>Freddie Mercury</color> from AIDS-related pneumonia. Next to this <color=#3366CC>Kurt Cobain</color>,

<color=#3366CC>Selena</color>, <color=#3366CC>Eazy-E</color>, <color=#3366CC>Tupac Shakur</color> and <color=#3366CC>the Notorious B.I.G.</color> were the most publicized music-related deaths of the decade,
in 1994, 1995, 1996, and 1997 respectively. Richey Edwards of Manic Street Preachers was publicized in the media in
1991 following an incident involving Steve Lamacq backstage after a live show, in which Edwards carved '4 Real' into
his arm. Edwards' disappearance in 1995 was highly publicized. He is still missing but was presumed dead in 2008.
